stem:
You are the paediatric resident on the ward. A 5 month old previously well infant was admitted 6 hours ago with a 3 day coryzal illness, cough, and increasing work of breathing. He is feeding at half his usual volumes and has had no apnoeas.

On assessment now he is alert and consolable in his father's arms. Chest auscultation reveals widespread fine crackles and expiratory wheeze. He has moderate subcostal recession, tracheal tug, and nasal flaring. He is not grunting.

Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 58, SpO2 88% in room air, temperature 37.8. Capillary blood gas shows pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L. Nasopharyngeal swab is positive for respiratory syncytial virus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 92/58, RR 58, SpO2 88% room air, temperature 37.8
data_table.Examination: Alert and consolable; widespread fine crackles and expiratory wheeze; moderate subcostal recession, tracheal tug, nasal flaring; no grunting
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.36, pCO2 44 mmHg (35-45), HCO3 24 mmol/L (22-32); NPA positive RSV
data_table.Feeding: 50% of usual volumes over past 12 hours; no apnoeas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Commence nasal prong oxygen at 1 to 2 L/min titrated to keep SpO2 at or above 90%
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance escalates in a stepwise fashion beginning with low flow nasal prong oxygen when SpO2 persistently drops below 90%; titration to a target of 90% avoids the harms of over oxygenation and prolonged admission (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Commence high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min and reassess in 1 to 2 hours
options.rationale: High flow nasal cannula is reserved for failure of low flow oxygen after an adequate trial or for infants with severe work of breathing; PARIS 1 showed no benefit as first line over standard oxygen (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back to back three times and reassess bronchodilator response
options.rationale: Nebulised bronchodilators are not recommended in typical bronchiolitis under 12 months because there is no sustained clinical benefit and they can worsen ventilation perfusion mismatch (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Escalate to bilevel non invasive ventilation because SpO2 remains below 90% in room air
options.rationale: Non invasive ventilation is a PICU level intervention considered after low flow and high flow trials fail with rising pCO2 or exhaustion; his gas and mental state do not yet warrant it (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

options.text: Continue room air observation with hourly work of breathing scoring and no supplemental oxygen
options.rationale: SpO2 persistently at 88% in room air with moderate recession meets the RCH threshold to commence supplemental oxygen; watchful waiting risks prolonged hypoxia (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis).

explanation.summary: Typical RSV bronchiolitis with hypoxia below 90% and moderate work of breathing. Australian practice starts low flow nasal prong oxygen titrated to a 90% target. HFNC and non invasive ventilation are reserved for failure of low flow. Bronchodilators are not routine in this age group.
key_points: RCH threshold to start oxygen is SpO2 persistently below 90%.
Low flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min is first line, not HFNC.
Bronchodilators and steroids are not recommended in typical bronchiolitis under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: For under 12 month bronchiolitis at RCH, low flow oxygen to a SpO2 target of 90% precedes any HFNC trial.

stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 2 year old is brought in at 2200 by his mother with a barking cough and hoarse voice that woke him. He is normally well and fully immunised.

In the cubicle he is settled on his mother's knee, drinking a small amount of water, with an audible barking cough between sentences. There is mild inspiratory stridor at rest that eases when he is quiet. Chest wall recession is limited to mild suprasternal indrawing. He is alert with normal colour.

Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 37.9. His mother declines nasal prong oxygen because it distresses him and reports no drooling or difficulty swallowing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 96/58, RR 34, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: Barking cough with hoarse voice; mild inspiratory stridor at rest that eases when quiet; mild suprasternal indrawing only; alert with normal colour
data_table.Feeding and swallow: Drinking water in cubicle; no drooling; no dysphagia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid regimen?

options.text: Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally once with disposition review at 30 minutes
options.rationale: The 0.6 mg/kg dose is reserved for severe croup with marked recession, hypoxia, agitation, or exhaustion; using it routinely in mild to moderate croup adds no efficacy and needless steroid exposure (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally once with disposition review at 30 minutes
options.rationale: RCH classifies stridor at rest with only mild recession as mild to moderate croup, for which 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone as a single dose is the recommended regimen (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg once with disposition review at 30 minutes
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is reserved for children who cannot tolerate the oral route; an alert 2 year old drinking water in the cubicle should receive oral dexamethasone (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg orally daily for 3 days with review before further doses
options.rationale: RCH and the CDC croup evidence base favour a single dose of dexamethasone over a prednisolone course because relapse rates are higher and duration of steroid exposure is longer (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

options.text: Withhold corticosteroids and observe for 4 hours before making a treatment decision
options.rationale: Stridor at rest is the threshold to give dexamethasone; delaying treatment prolongs symptoms and extends emergency length of stay (Source: RCH CPG: Croup).

explanation.summary: Stridor at rest with only mild recession fits the RCH mild to moderate croup band. Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once is standard; 0.6 mg/kg is reserved for severe cases. Nebulised budesonide is a route substitute, not a preferred first agent. Prednisolone courses are inferior to single dose dexamethasone.
key_points: Dose 0.15 mg/kg for mild to moderate croup at RCH.
Reserve 0.6 mg/kg for severe croup (marked recession, hypoxia, agitation).
Oral dexamethasone is preferred over nebulised budesonide when tolerated.
explanation.pearls: The RCH severity to dose rule is dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild to moderate croup and 0.6 mg/kg only for severe.

sources.label: Bjornson et al. Cochrane review: Nebulised epinephrine for croup

subtopic_detail: UTI imaging after first typical episode
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 14 month old girl in outpatients 2 weeks after her first admission with pyelonephritis. She was fully immunised, was born at term after uncomplicated antenatal ultrasounds, and has had no prior infections.

During admission urine culture grew Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim. She defervesced within 24 hours of intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin and completed oral cefalexin at home. Renal function and electrolytes on discharge were within normal limits.

Today she is thriving on the paediatric growth centiles. Her parents ask what imaging she needs. Antenatal renal ultrasounds at 20 and 32 weeks were reported as normal.

data_table.Growth: Weight and height on the 50th centile
data_table.Illness course: Defervesced within 24 hours of IV antibiotics; oral course completed
data_table.Renal function: Discharge creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What imaging is most appropriate now?

options.text: Arrange a DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months to look for renal cortical scarring in this child
options.rationale: DMSA scanning is not part of the RCH cascade for a first typical UTI and adds radiation without changing management for a well thriving child (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Arrange an outpatient renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks to exclude an anatomical abnormality
options.rationale: RCH does not recommend routine ultrasound after a first typical UTI in a child older than 6 months with normal antenatal imaging; this is a NICE style pathway not adopted by RCH (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Reassure the family that no routine renal tract imaging is required after this first typical UTI
options.rationale: RCH restricts routine ultrasound to atypical UTI, recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without documented normal antenatal scans; a typical single UTI in a well infant older than 6 months does not require imaging (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Arrange a micturating cystourethrogram to grade reflux before considering long term prophylaxis
options.rationale: MCUG is invasive and is not first line for a single typical UTI in an older infant; RCH reserves it for selected atypical or recurrent cases after ultrasound findings (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

options.text: Commence long term oral trimethoprim prophylaxis until an outpatient specialist review takes place
options.rationale: Antibiotic prophylaxis after a first typical UTI has minimal benefit in preventing scarring and RCH does not recommend it routinely for a well child (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection).

explanation.summary: A well thriving 14 month old with a first typical UTI, normal antenatal scans, and prompt defervescence needs no routine imaging under the RCH cascade. Imaging is reserved for atypical or recurrent UTI, or infants under 6 months without antenatal monitoring. DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs, not part of the RCH pathway.
key_points: RCH does not recommend routine ultrasound after a single typical UTI over 6 months old.
Atypical features (poor response after 48 hours, non E coli, sepsis, mass, raised creatinine) trigger imaging.
DMSA and MCUG are not part of the RCH first UTI cascade.
explanation.pearls: Under RCH, a single typical UTI in a well child over 6 months of age with normal antenatal scans requires no routine imaging.

subtopic_detail: Rehydration route after failed oral rehydration
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar. An 18 month old boy has had 2 days of loose watery bowel motions and vomiting. His mother has been offering oral rehydration solution at home but he continues to vomit small amounts within 10 minutes of every offer.

In the department he is alert but tired, with sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes. Capillary refill is 3 seconds centrally and skin turgor is reduced. Peripheries are warm. He weighs 11 kg, previously 12 kg.

Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 37.6. He has just received a single oral dose of ondansetron 2 mg and again vomited a 30 mL sip of oral rehydration solution 15 minutes later.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 92/54, RR 28, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.6
data_table.Weight: 11 kg today; 12 kg at well child check 3 weeks ago (approximately 8% loss)
data_table.Examination: Alert but tired; sunken eyes; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 seconds centrally; reduced skin turgor; warm peripheries
data_table.Interventions so far: Ondansetron 2 mg oral 15 minutes ago; 30 mL oral rehydration solution vomited again

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Admit for observation and offer clear fluids ad libitum without a structured rehydration plan
options.rationale: Ad libitum sipping in a child who repeatedly vomits does not correct the estimated 8% deficit in a defined time and lengthens admission (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).

options.text: Cannulate and give a 20 mL/kg intravenous saline bolus followed by intravenous maintenance fluids
options.rationale: Intravenous rehydration is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or failure of nasogastric rehydration; this child is not shocked and has not yet had an NGT trial (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).

options.text: Give a further oral dose of ondansetron 2 mg and continue small volume oral rehydration solution sips
options.rationale: A single ondansetron dose is the RCH recommended maximum; repeat oral dosing has no evidence and delays effective rehydration in a child already failing the oral route (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and rehydrate at 25 mL/kg/hour of oral rehydration solution for 4 hours with electrolyte review
options.rationale: For mild to moderate dehydration where oral rehydration has failed, RCH prefers nasogastric rehydration ahead of intravenous fluids because it corrects deficit safely and avoids cannulation morbidity (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).

options.text: Give an intramuscular metoclopramide 0.15 mg/kg dose to control vomiting before further oral trials
options.rationale: Metoclopramide is not first line for paediatric gastroenteritis vomiting in Australia because of extrapyramidal risk; ondansetron is preferred but NGT is the escalation when it fails (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration).

explanation.summary: This child has mild to moderate dehydration with failed oral rehydration despite a single dose of ondansetron. RCH prefers nasogastric rehydration next, at 25 mL/kg/hour for 4 hours, before intravenous fluids. IV therapy is reserved for shock, severe dehydration, or NGT failure.
key_points: NGT rehydration is first line after failed oral rehydration for mild to moderate dehydration.
Ondansetron dose in this age group is a single dose only.
IV rehydration is reserved for shock, severe dehydration, or NGT failure.
explanation.pearls: For mild to moderate paediatric dehydration that fails oral rehydration, the RCH next step is nasogastric rehydration at 25 mL/kg/hour, not intravenous fluids.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar. A 5 week old term boy is brought in by his parents for feeding poorly for the past 6 hours and one episode of vomiting.

He was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery. His mother was group B streptococcus positive on antenatal screening but received two doses of intrapartum benzylpenicillin. Antenatal serology, including hepatitis and syphilis, was within normal limits.

On examination he is pale, mottled to the knees, and only briefly responsive to handling. Anterior fontanelle is soft; there is no rash. Chest is clear and abdomen is soft. Capillary refill is 3 seconds centrally. Peripheries are cool.

Vital signs: pulse 178, blood pressure 68/38, respiratory rate 62, SpO2 94% in room air, temperature 38.4. Point of care glucose is 3.4 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178, BP 68/38, RR 62, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Examination: Pale, mottled to knees, only briefly responsive; anterior fontanelle soft; no rash; capillary refill 3 seconds; cool peripheries
data_table.Antenatal: Term normal vaginal delivery; mother GBS positive with 2 doses intrapartum benzylpenicillin; hepatitis and syphilis serology within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial workup and empirical antibiotic plan?

options.text: Observation on the paediatric ward for 24 hours without immediate empirical antibiotics or lumbar puncture
options.rationale: An unwell appearing febrile infant under 3 months requires empirical antibiotics within the first hour after cultures; observation alone would delay life saving treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Blood culture, urine, and oral amoxicillin as an outpatient with 24 hour paediatric review
options.rationale: Outpatient oral antibiotics are inappropriate for a febrile infant under 3 months, and an unwell appearance mandates admission with intravenous therapy (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Blood culture and urine only, deferring lumbar puncture until CRP and procalcitonin results
options.rationale: Under 3 months, biomarker guided deferral of lumbar puncture is not recommended by RCH; occult meningitis has been missed with a strategy that waits for inflammatory markers (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Blood culture, urine, chest x ray, and empirical intravenous ceftriaxone with lumbar puncture only if unwell
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is avoided in the neonatal period because of ceftriaxone calcium precipitation and unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia risks; cefotaxime with benzylpenicillin is preferred (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

options.text: Full septic workup including blood culture, urine, and lumbar puncture, then intravenous cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin
options.rationale: For a febrile infant under 3 months, particularly one who is unwell appearing, RCH mandates full septic screening including CSF and empirical intravenous cefotaxime with benzylpenicillin to cover Listeria (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child).

explanation.summary: An unwell febrile infant under 3 months needs a full septic workup, including lumbar puncture, and empirical intravenous cefotaxime with benzylpenicillin to cover Listeria in the neonatal age band. Ceftriaxone is avoided at this age because of bilirubin displacement and calcium precipitation risk. Outpatient oral antibiotics, biomarker guided deferral of the CSF sample, and pure observation all delay definitive treatment in a window where mortality rises hour by hour.
key_points: Under 3 months: full septic screen including CSF for any unwell appearance.
Cover Listeria with benzylpenicillin plus cefotaxime under 4 to 6 weeks.
Avoid ceftriaxone in the neonatal period.
explanation.pearls: For an unwell febrile infant under 3 months, RCH gives cefotaxime plus benzylpenicillin, not ceftriaxone, alongside a full septic screen including lumbar puncture.
